part2.intro: Three young people talk about their favourite place in nature.
part2.question: For each question, choose the correct answer.

texts.label: A
texts.title: Freya
texts.text: My favourite place is a small lake in the mountains in the north of Scotland. We go there every summer and stay in a wooden house near the water. The lake is really cold, even in August, but I still swim in it every morning. At night there are no lights anywhere, so you can see thousands of stars in the sky. I've never seen anything so beautiful.

texts.label: B
texts.title: Kofi
texts.text: There's a forest only ten minutes from my house, and I go there almost every weekend with my dog. I know every path. In spring the ground is covered in blue flowers, and in autumn the trees turn red and gold. Last year I helped the forest workers to plant two hundred young trees. I'd like to work outdoors like them when I leave school.

texts.label: C
texts.title: Thao
texts.text: My grandparents live on a small island in the south of Vietnam. You can only get there by boat, and there are no cars on the island at all! I love walking along the beach and exploring the rocks. My cousin taught me to fish in the sea. It's very hot in summer, so we have a rest in the afternoon and go out again in the evening.

part3.title: The boy who saved his river
part3.text:
When thirteen-year-old Ollie Grant went fishing with his grandfather last spring, he didn't catch any fish. Instead, he pulled three plastic bags and an old shoe out of the river.

"I was really angry," Ollie says. "My grandad told me that when he was a boy, the water was so clean you could see the fish swimming. Now it's brown and full of rubbish."

Ollie decided to do something. He made a poster and put it up in the town library. It asked people to help him clean the river on Saturday mornings. "I thought maybe five people would come," he says. "But on the first day, forty people were there – children, parents, even my head teacher!"

Since then, the group has taken more than two hundred bags of rubbish out of the river. They have also planted trees and flowers along the sides of the river. "Trees are important because they give shade, and that keeps the water cool for the fish," Ollie explains.

It isn't always easy. "In winter it's freezing, and our hands get really cold. Some weeks only a few people come. But I never want to stop."

The work is making a difference. Last month, Ollie and his grandfather went fishing in the same place. This time Ollie caught a fish – and there was no plastic anywhere.

"It was the best day ever," he smiles. "Now I want to help clean every river in the country!"

part4.title: Antarctica
part4.text:
Antarctica is the coldest place in the {19}. It is at the bottom of the Earth, around the South Pole, and about ninety-eight per cent of it is {20} with ice. In some places, the ice is more than four kilometres thick!

Nobody lives in Antarctica all the time, but about four thousand scientists go there in summer. They study the ice, the sea and the animals that live there, such as penguins. In winter, only about a thousand people {21} because the weather is too dangerous. The sun doesn't {22} for weeks, and it is dark all day.

There are no trees or flowers, but some very small plants can {23} on the rocks. Antarctica is also a great place to look at the night sky, because the air is so clean.

People first {24} Antarctica about two hundred years ago. Today, a few thousand tourists visit it every year by ship.

items.q: Which animal did the boy see in the forest?

script.t: Did you see any animals on your walk in the forest, Tom?
We hoped to see some rabbits, but there weren't any.
That's a shame. What about birds?
We heard lots of them, but they were too high up in the trees to see. But when we stopped for lunch by the river, a fox came really close to us! I took a photo.

items.q: What will the weather be like on the mountain tomorrow?

script.t: Shall we climb the mountain tomorrow?
Let me check the weather. Today it's raining, but tomorrow it'll be sunny all day.
Will there be any snow at the top?
Not now, it's summer! There was snow up there in May, but it's all gone.

items.q: Where will the family have their picnic?

script.t: Where shall we have our picnic? By the lake?
There are too many people there on Sundays. What about the top of the hill? The view's amazing.
It's a long walk with all this food!
OK, then. What about the field next to the farm? There's a big tree there, so we can sit in the shade.
Perfect.

items.q: What is the boy growing in the school garden?

script.t: What are you growing in your part of the school garden, Ryan?
I wanted to grow tomatoes, but Mr Clark said our garden is too cold for them.
So what are you growing?
Sunflowers! They can grow really tall – maybe two metres. Next year I'm going to try strawberries.

items.q: How did the girl get to the island?

script.t: How did you get to the island? By boat?
That's how most people go. But in the morning the sea goes out a long way, and you can walk across the sand.
Really?
Yes! We walked there in the morning. But we had to come back by boat in the afternoon, because the water came back.

part2.intro: You will hear a guide talking to a group of students about a day at a forest centre.
part2.title: A Day at Greenwood Forest Centre

script.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Greenwood Forest Centre. Here's the plan for today. First, you can leave your bags in the classroom. Our walk through the forest starts at a quarter past ten, so you've got fifteen minutes to get ready. The walk is six kilometres. Some groups do the long walk to the top of the hill – that's ten kilometres – but it's too far for today. On the way, we'll look at the different trees and plants, and if you're quiet, you might see some deer. At about half past twelve we'll stop for lunch next to the river. Please don't go into the water – it's deeper than it looks! In the afternoon, you're going to help us plant trees. Every year about a thousand trees in this forest are lost because of strong winds, so we need your help. We'll give you gloves, but please wear old shoes or boots. My name's Kate Morrow, and I'll be your guide today. That's M-O-R-R-O-W. If you have any questions, just ask me. OK, let's go!

part3.intro: You will hear Ben talking to his friend Lucy about his summer holiday on a farm.

items.q: Where is the farm?
What did Ben do every morning?
What surprised Ben about the farm?
options: how quiet it was at night

items.q: What didn't Ben like about the farm?
When will Ben go to the farm again?

script.t: Hi Ben! You look really brown. Where have you been?
I spent three weeks on my uncle's farm in the countryside.
Is that in the north, near the mountains?
No, it's in the west, near the sea. My uncle used to live in the south, but he moved there five years ago.
So what did you do there all day?
Lots! Every morning I got up at six and helped to give food to the sheep. In the afternoons I sometimes worked in the fields, but only when it wasn't too hot. And once or twice we went to the beach.
Was the work hard?

Not really. But the thing that surprised me was how quiet it was. At home in the city there's always noise from cars. On the farm, at night, I could only hear the wind in the trees. And the sky was full of stars.
Was there anything you didn't like?
The weather was perfect and my aunt's food was great. But the insects were terrible, especially near the river in the evenings. I've still got bites everywhere!
Will you go back?
Definitely. My uncle wants me to come in the spring, when the baby sheep are born. But I can't, because I've got exams. So I'll go next summer again, and maybe I'll take my sister.

script.t: Dad, can you help me with my science project?

items.q: How did the boy feel at the end of the walk?

script.t: Yesterday I climbed Snow Hill with my brother. It took four hours to get to the top, and my legs really hurt. When we got there, there was so much cloud that we couldn't see anything! But I didn't mind. It's the highest hill in our area, and I did it. I'm really pleased with myself.

items.q: What must the students NOT do?

script.t: Right, everyone, we're in the forest now. You can take as many photos of the flowers as you like, but please don't pick them. Leave them for other people to enjoy. In this part of the forest, you don't have to stay on the paths – you're free to explore. But stay where you can see a teacher, please.

script.t: It's so cold today. The news says it might snow tonight.
I hope it does! I don't want to make a snowman or anything – I'm too old for that.
Ha! So you want school to close?
No, I like school! I want to take photos of the hills when they're white. It's for a photo competition.

script.t: Tonight at eight, don't miss Wild World. This week, the team travels to a small island in the far north, where it's winter for nine months of the year. They'll show you how the birds there find food on the ice and snow. And next week, the team visits a hot desert in Africa.

part5.intro: You will hear Nam talking to his teacher about the class nature project. What will each student make a poster about?

script.t: Right, Nam, you're helping me with the list. Let's check who's doing what for the nature project. Lily wanted to do flowers, didn't she?
She did, Miss, but Sara chose flowers first. So Lily's doing mountains. She climbed one with her family in the summer, so she's got lots of photos.
So Sara's doing flowers. Good. What about Omar? Islands, wasn't it?
He was going to, but he couldn't find enough information. He's doing rivers now. He lives next to a big one, so he can go and look at it.
Great. And Duc?
Duc's really interested in space. He wanted to do the moon, but you said there wasn't enough to write about. So he's doing stars.
Oh yes, I remember. And you, Nam? Are you doing the sea?
I was going to do forests, but Lily's sister did forests last year, and I want something different. So I'm doing ice – you know, in the far north and the south of the world.
Excellent. That's an interesting topic. Get started, then!
